The main finding is that our original news-tone measure adds little dependable forecasting information once broader conditions and previous sentiment are included. But this is also a measurement study. Source selection changes the economic issues the text represents, and classifier transfer limits confidence in the labels. I will focus on those NLP findings and then show what the original text measure contributes to the regressions. The economic baseline leaves a gap, but that gap alone cannot identify its cause.
An original text index links titles to sentiment

The corpus contains 670 relevant economic titles from national reporting, state reporting, and forum submissions. Automated coding assigns minus one for adverse economic direction, zero for mixed or undirected claims, and plus one for favorable direction. Topic and price-framing measures use fixed wording rules, while selected factual cases use official-release benchmarks. Within each month, I average labels within each source and then give the three sources equal weight. That produces 47 balanced monthly readings. Timing leaves 45 usable observations and 21 evaluation targets. The original NLP index therefore enters the statistical analysis directly.
Classifier transfer limits confidence in tone

The classifier comparison is a substantive NLP result. A hybrid combining semantic features with conventional text classification achieves 68 percent agreement with automated reference labels in grouped development evaluation. On a new set of 300 titles, that falls to 53.3 percent. The reference sets differ, so this is a transfer check rather than a matched accuracy comparison. It warns against assuming that development performance generalizes. The final primary index uses frozen automated title coding and remains provisional. Repeated coding consistency does not establish independent accuracy.

The text measurements also reveal differences in source emphasis. Housing vocabulary appears in about 31 percent of the Colorado Sun sample, compared with about 10 percent of Hacker News titles. Inflation-rate wording shows the opposite pattern: about 20 percent for Hacker News and 3 percent for Colorado Sun. These differences matter because a tone index partly reflects which economic issues its sources cover. Equal source weighting controls volume shifts, but it cannot make the selected sources representative of all US media. These are overlapping vocabulary measures within sampled titles, rather than evidence of reader bias.
News helps only the narrower model

These bars compare forecast errors on the same 21 target months. Lower RMSE means smaller mistakes in sentiment index points. Adding original tone to the simple economic model reduces error from 12.07 to 10.82. However, the uncertainty interval around that improvement includes zero. The broader comparison changes the interpretation. Controls without tone achieve 5.82, while adding tone gives 6.06. So the larger improvement over the economic baseline is already present without news. Multiple linear regression gives each predictor a separate slope, and the matched comparison holds the other predictors constant. It provides little support for an additional forecasting contribution from our primary tone measure.
Last month already tells us a great deal

Sentiment persistence makes the benchmark more demanding. Predicting last month unchanged gives an error of 4.09. Broader controls plus previous sentiment give 3.98. Adding original tone increases error to 4.32. This suggests that the measure supplies little dependable extra forecasting information once those inputs are included. The result concerns this measure and this short sample. It does not establish that news never influences sentiment. Revised historical inputs and a previously inspected test period also make this a retrospective evaluation rather than a fresh real-time forecast test.
Different wording can describe the same fact

The factual cases show why economic direction and bias need separate evidence. In the July 2020 GDP release, a 32.9 percent annualized decline corresponds to about a 9.5 percent decline over the actual quarter. Both magnitudes can describe the same event. The units and context determine how to interpret them. A title can describe an adverse economic fact accurately, while an omitted unit can create ambiguity. These examples support careful factual calibration, but they cannot establish how common biased coverage is or how readers respond. That would require a broader event benchmark and corresponding audience evidence.

The practical implication is to monitor tone alongside household pressures and investigate unusual sentiment gaps. Our primary text signal does not yet demonstrate dependable additional forecast value. A dictionary sensitivity improves one secondary result, so I retain that contrary evidence as exploratory. The selected corpus, provisional labels, and revised historical data limit confidence. We also lack audience exposure. A stronger causal test would randomize equally truthful summaries emphasizing price levels, inflation rates, or balanced context. The report proposes 600 participants, but no experiment has run. The contribution is a transparent connection from original text measurements to matched forecast tests, with measurement failures and uncertainty kept visible. Thank you.
